column1: State the iron law of performance.
column2: CPU time = instruction count × CPI / clock frequency (equivalently × cycle time).

column1: What does Amdahl's law say, and what is its limit?
column2: Speedup = 1/((1−p) + p/N) for a parallel fraction p on N units; it can never exceed 1/(1−p).

column1: How does Gustafson's view differ from Amdahl's?
column2: It grows the problem with the machine, so scaled speedup = (1−p) + pN keeps rising.

column1: Write the dynamic power equation.
column2: P = αCV²f: activity, switched capacitance, supply voltage squared, clock frequency.

column1: Why did clock frequencies stop rising around the mid-2000s?
column2: Supply voltage stopped scaling (the end of Dennard scaling), so higher frequency meant unsustainable power density.

column1: What is a fair way to compare two machines' speed?
column2: Run the same workload and compare total execution time (or its reciprocal), not MIPS or clock rate alone.

column1: What are the six RV32I instruction formats?
column2: R, I, S, B, U and J; rd, rs1 and rs2 keep the same bit positions in every format.

column1: Why is the immediate's sign always in bit 31 in RISC-V?
column2: So sign extension can start before decoding finishes, simplifying and speeding the hardware.

column1: How do you load an arbitrary 32-bit constant in RV32I?
column2: lui for the upper 20 bits, then addi for the lower 12 (adding 1 to the upper part if bit 11 of the constant is set).

column1: What is the reach of a RISC-V conditional branch?
column2: ±4 KiB (13-bit signed byte offset, always even); jal reaches ±1 MiB.

column1: How do RISC-V, Arm and x86 differ as businesses?
column2: RISC-V is an open standard anyone can implement; Arm licenses cores and architectures for fees and royalties; x86 is effectively held by Intel and AMD under their cross-licence.

column1: Why does x86 decoding cost more than RISC-V decoding?
column2: Variable-length instructions (1 to 15 bytes) must be found and decoded serially or speculatively.

column1: Which RISC-V registers must a callee preserve?
column2: s0–s11 and sp (callee-saved); t0–t6, a0–a7 and ra are caller-saved.

column1: Why must the stack pointer stay 16-byte aligned in the RISC-V ABI?
column2: The psABI requires it at calls so that wide data types and spills are naturally aligned.

column1: What does the linker do with relocations?
column2: It fills in addresses that the assembler could not know (calls, globals) once sections are placed.

column1: What is linker relaxation in RISC-V?
column2: Replacing a two-instruction auipc+jalr call with a single jal when the target turns out to be in range.

column1: Why does a leaf function often need no stack frame?
column2: It calls nothing, so it need not save ra, and it can work in caller-saved registers.

column1: When does two's-complement addition overflow?
column2: When both operands have the same sign and the result has the other sign.

column1: What is the FP32 format?
column2: 1 sign bit, 8 exponent bits (bias 127), 23 fraction bits: (−1)^s × 1.f × 2^(e−127) for normal numbers.

column1: What is bfloat16?
column2: The top 16 bits of FP32: same 8-bit exponent and range, 7 fraction bits of precision.

column1: Why can summing many floating-point numbers lose accuracy, and what helps?
column2: Each addition rounds; pairwise (tree) or compensated (Kahan) summation keep the error growth small.

column1: How does division by a constant become a multiplication?
column2: Multiply by a precomputed 'magic' reciprocal and shift, which compilers derive so the result equals the exact quotient.

column1: What is a block (microscaling) format such as MX?
column2: A block of low-precision values shares one scale factor (exponent), giving range with few bits per value.

column1: What sets the clock period of a single-cycle processor?
column2: The slowest instruction's path, usually the load (instruction memory, register read, ALU, data memory, write-back).

column1: What does the main decoder produce?
column2: The control signals (RegWrite, ALUSrc, MemRead/Write, MemToReg, Branch, ALUOp) from the opcode.

column1: Why is a single-cycle design inefficient?
column2: Every instruction takes as long as the slowest one, so fast instructions waste most of the cycle.

column1: What are the five classic pipeline stages?
column2: IF, ID, EX, MEM, WB.

column1: How many cycles does the five-stage pipeline take for N instructions?
column2: N + 4 + S + 2T with S load-use stalls and T taken branches resolved in EX.

column1: Why does a load-use hazard still stall with forwarding?
column2: The loaded value exists only after MEM, one cycle too late for the next instruction's EX.

column1: What limits pipeline depth?
column2: Pipeline-register overhead per stage, unbalanced stages, and larger branch and hazard penalties.

column1: What are the three kinds of pipeline hazard?
column2: Structural (resource conflicts), data (dependences) and control (branches).

column1: How does a misprediction affect CPI?
column2: Adds (branch fraction) × (misprediction rate) × (penalty), or MPKI/1000 × penalty.

column1: Why use 2-bit counters instead of 1-bit?
column2: Hysteresis: a single anomalous outcome (such as a loop exit) does not flip the prediction.

column1: What does gshare do?
column2: XORs global branch history with the PC to index the counter table, capturing correlations between branches.

column1: What are the BTB and the return-address stack for?
column2: The BTB supplies predicted targets at fetch; the RAS predicts return addresses by pushing at calls and popping at returns.

column1: What is Spectre variant 1 in one sentence?
column2: A mispredicted bounds check lets speculative code read out of bounds and leak the value through cache timing.

column1: Why can removing a branch beat predicting it?
column2: Data-dependent branches on random data mispredict often; branchless code (select, arithmetic) pays no misprediction penalty.

column1: Which dependences does register renaming remove?
column2: WAR and WAW (name dependences); RAW true dependences remain.

column1: What is the dataflow limit?
column2: Execution time with unlimited resources and perfect prediction: the latency-weighted critical path of true dependences.

column1: What does the reorder buffer guarantee?
column2: In-order retirement, so exceptions and mispredictions are precise despite out-of-order execution.

column1: How large must the window be to hide latency L at width w?
column2: About w × L entries, by Little's law.

column1: Why does pointer chasing not speed up with issue width?
column2: Each address depends on the previous load, so the chain of load latencies sets the time.

column1: What does a load/store queue do?
column2: Keeps stores in order, forwards store data to dependent loads, and lets independent loads pass older stores.

column1: Distinguish temporal and spatial locality.
column2: Temporal: recently used data is used again soon. Spatial: data near recently used data is used soon.

column1: How do you split an address for a cache?
column2: offset = log2(block), index = log2(sets), sets = capacity/(block × ways), tag = the remaining high bits.

column1: Write the two-level AMAT formula.
column2: AMAT = t1 + m1 (t2 + m2,local × t_mem).

column1: Name the three Cs of cache misses.
column2: Compulsory (first touch), capacity (working set too big), conflict (too many blocks in one set).

column1: When is write-back better than write-through?
column2: When blocks are written repeatedly: write-back writes each dirty block once, at eviction.

column1: Why does tiling speed up matrix multiplication?
column2: It reuses tiles that fit in the cache many times before eviction, cutting misses by large factors.

column1: How does memory-level parallelism set bandwidth?
column2: Bandwidth = outstanding misses × block size / latency (Little's law).

column1: What is HBM?
column2: Stacked DRAM dies on an interposer beside the processor with a very wide interface (1024 bits, 2048 in HBM4), giving about 1–2 TB/s per stack.

column1: What does virtual memory provide?
column2: Isolation, protection, relocation and demand paging by translating virtual pages to physical frames.

column1: How does Sv32 split a virtual address?
column2: VPN[1] bits 31–22, VPN[0] bits 21–12, page offset bits 11–0; two levels of 1024 four-byte PTEs.

column1: When is a PTE a leaf?
column2: When R or X is set; with R = W = X = 0 it points to the next level.

column1: What is TLB reach?
column2: Entries × page size: the memory a TLB can map without missing.

column1: Why are page tables multilevel?
column2: Flat tables need an entry per virtual page; radix trees allocate tables only for regions in use.

column1: What constrains a VIPT L1 cache's size?
column2: Size / associativity must not exceed the page size, so the index uses only untranslated bits.

column1: Where does execution resume after a page fault versus an ecall?
column2: After a fault, at the faulting instruction (mepc); after an ecall, at mepc + 4.

column1: What is thrashing?
column2: When the working set exceeds physical memory, nearly every access faults and the system pages instead of computing.

column1: What is Belady's anomaly?
column2: Under FIFO replacement, adding frames can increase page faults; stack algorithms such as LRU cannot show it.

column1: What is memory-mapped I/O?
column2: Device registers occupy physical addresses and are accessed with loads and stores (uncached, ordered, volatile).

column1: When do interrupts beat polling?
column2: When events are infrequent; polling wins when events arrive faster than interrupt overhead allows.

column1: What does interrupt coalescing trade?
column2: Fewer interrupts (less CPU time) for added latency.

column1: What problem does DMA create, and how is it solved?
column2: Writes to memory behind the caches' backs; solved by coherent DMA or explicit cache flush/invalidate.

column1: State the AXI handshake rule.
column2: A transfer happens when VALID and READY are both high; a sender must not wait for READY before asserting VALID.

column1: How do you compute PCIe bandwidth per direction?
column2: GT/s × lanes × encoding efficiency / 8 (128b/130b from PCIe 3.0; Flits and FEC from 6.0).

column1: Average hops in a k × k mesh?
column2: 2(k² − 1)/(3k) ≈ 2k/3 for uniform traffic.

column1: State the two coherence invariants.
column2: Single writer or multiple readers per block at any time; every read returns the latest write.

column1: What does MESI's E state save?
column2: A silent upgrade to M on write for data no other core holds: one bus transaction instead of two.

column1: Snooping or directory: when each?
column2: Snooping for a few to a few dozen cores on a broadcast medium; directories for larger systems.

column1: What is false sharing?
column2: Coherence misses from different cores writing different words in the same cache block.

column1: What is sequential consistency?
column2: Every execution acts like one interleaving of all threads' operations, each thread in program order.

column1: What does TSO relax, and which test shows it?
column2: A store followed by a load to another address; the store-buffering test can give r1 = r2 = 0.

column1: Why is test-and-test-and-set better than test-and-set?
column2: Spinning on reads stays in the local cache (S state); spinning on swaps invalidates every waiter each time.

column1: What do LR/SC do?
column2: LR loads and reserves; SC stores only if the reservation still holds, returning 0 on success.

column1: SIMD versus SIMT?
column2: SIMD exposes vector instructions; SIMT runs scalar threads grouped into warps that share an instruction stream.

column1: What does divergence cost?
column2: A warp executes each taken path in turn with other lanes masked, lowering SIMD efficiency.

column1: What makes a warp's access coalesced?
column2: Consecutive threads accessing consecutive addresses, so few 32-byte sectors are touched.

column1: Shared-memory bank-conflict degree for stride s?
column2: gcd(s, 32); padding a 32-word row to 33 removes column conflicts.

column1: What limits occupancy?
column2: Registers per thread, shared memory per block, and the SM's warp and block slots.

column1: How many warps hide latency L with k instructions between waits?
column2: About 1 + L/k per scheduler.

column1: Dense versus sparse tensor throughput?
column2: Sparse figures assume 2:4 structured sparsity and are twice the dense rate.

column1: Why do neural networks suit accelerators?
column2: Dominated by multiply-accumulate on large matrices with regular access, high reuse and tolerance of low precision.

column1: How long does an output-stationary systolic array take for M×K by K×N?
column2: K + M + N − 2 cycles.

column1: Why skew a systolic array's inputs?
column2: So a_ik and b_kj reach PE (i, j) in the same cycle, k + i + j.

column1: What is a weight-stationary dataflow?
column2: Weights stay in the PEs while inputs stream through, reusing each weight across a batch.

column1: How much reuse makes data movement cheaper than an INT8 MAC (45 nm)?
column2: About 22 from a 32 KB SRAM and about 1400 from DRAM.

column1: SQNR rule of thumb for quantization?
column2: About 6 dB per bit: 6.02b + 1.76 dB for a full-scale sinusoid.

column1: Why is LLM decoding at batch 1 memory-bound?
column2: About 1 FLOP per byte of BF16 weights, far below ridge points of hundreds of FLOP/byte.

column1: State the roofline.
column2: Attainable = min(peak compute, bandwidth × arithmetic intensity); the ridge point is peak / bandwidth.

column1: How do you tell if a kernel is memory-bound?
column2: Its FLOP per byte of memory traffic is below the machine's ridge point.

column1: Why does SPEC use the geometric mean?
column2: The geometric mean of ratios equals the ratio of geometric means, so comparisons do not depend on the reference machine.

column1: SPEC base versus peak?
column2: Base (mandatory): same flags for all benchmarks in a language; peak (optional): per-benchmark flags and feedback-directed optimization.

column1: MLPerf Closed versus Open?
column2: Closed requires the reference model and processing (comparing systems); Open allows any model or method and must be labelled 'MLPerf Open'.

column1: When is the harmonic mean right?
column2: For averaging rates over equal amounts of work (total work / total time).

column1: Name four ways benchmark claims are inflated.
column2: Peak instead of delivered, sparse or low-precision figures, benchmark-specific tuning, and cherry-picked workloads, batch sizes or scenarios.
